lines.note: Continues the preceding definition with spun thread or silk thread. Vacu wo kuru introduces operating the reel; the attached object particle uo belongs to the Japanese example.
The Portuguese describes working this reel. The scan supports Andar and ſarilho, correcting the OCR's final e and ch; ito- begins the thread-object phrase continued below.
Ito-uo completes the object 'thread', and kuritsukuru describes winding it onto the frame. The gloss says to wind the thread and put it on the reel; printed Debar is retained without modernization.
Sarilho completes the Portuguese prepositional phrase 'on the reel'. This short continuation is a separate physical body row.
Wakugoo is glossed by 'erring deeds' and by bad or depraved actions. The visible circumflexes in Vacugô and Madô are retained; de- begins depravadas on the next row.

runs.text: prauadas, ou feitas ao contrario do que ſe de-

lines.note: Completes depraved actions and adds actions done contrary to what should have been done. Both divisions, de-prauadas and de-uião, follow the actual physical rows.
The opening fragment completes deuião, finishing 'what ought to have been done'. This is the close of the moral-action definition, not an independent entry.

runs.text: O declarar, ou traduzir as palauras

lines.note: Wakun denotes explaining or translating words into Japanese vernacular readings. The Portuguese begins with declaring or translating, whose object is continued below.

runs.text: Chinas, & cobitas em palauras brandas de

lines.note: Continues with Chinese and learned or refined words, contrasted with plain Japanese. Cobitas is the Portuguese plural of the Japanese-derived term kobita, not an OCR accident; Collado's grammar discusses this learned Chinese-derived vocabulary (Spear translation, pp. 171–172 and note 62: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/21197/21197-h/21197-h.htm). The printed italic word is retained and flagged for optional typeface review.

Completes the reference to Japan and introduces wakun ni tenzuru, converting to Japanese readings. The final o of Iapão is abraded on its left: its surviving curved right flank and the country-name context support o rather than OCR s; the following gloss describes supplying reading marks or letters.

runs.text: ou letras às palauras da China pera ſe ler em

lines.note: The reading marks or letters are added to Chinese words so that they can be read in Japanese. The continuous palauras corrects the OCR's spurious split pala tras.
The target is ordinary Japanese language. A second illustration, wakun ni yomu, begins here and is divided after yo- across the physical line break.

runs.text: Ler as letras Chinas com palauras brã-

lines.note: Mu completes yomu, reading Chinese characters through plain Japanese words. The nasal abbreviation in brã- belongs to the Portuguese brã-das division.
Completes the phrase 'plain words of Japan', ending the wakun entry. The final country name preserves the printed Portuguese nasal spelling.
Wakuran denotes confusion or disturbance, with madoi and midaruru furnishing Japanese explanatory forms. Perturbação begins the corresponding Portuguese pair of meanings.
Perplexidade adds perplexity; wakuran suru is then glossed as being disturbed or confused. The initial long s of ſuru is visible and is not an f.
Completes estar: 'disturbed or perplexed'. The scan resolves the OCR's separated perturba lo and perolexo to perturbado and perplexo.
Wakurawa is equated with marena, something rare. P. is the poetry label, with its sloping letter retained in the italic span rather than expanding the abbreviation.
Wakurawani is the adverbial form of the preceding adjective, hence 'rarely'. The printed entry supplies only Adu., and no explanatory words are invented.
Wadakamari and its principal forms introduce concealed or dissembling behavior. The gloss's refo- continues as refolhado, which figuratively describes a hidden or folded-in disposition.

Completes refolhado and gives an example of a person with a concealed or resentful heart. The printed Cocoruno is preserved despite the expected kokoro no construction; the Japanese example remains upright.

Translates the preceding example as a malicious, dissembling man. Malicioſo and refolhado are continuous italic Portuguese words, correcting fragmented OCR typography; Iaga begins the separate snake example.
Ja ga wadakamatte woru describes a snake lying coiled. The Portuguese starts 'the snake or serpent being', with ser- continuing onto the next physical row.
Completes serpente and specifies being coiled, with the gloss's added notion of malice. This links the physical coiling sense to the preceding figurative concealment sense.
The noun wadakamari is glossed as malice or hidden reservation. It restates the figurative meaning after the preceding verb and snake illustration.
Wadan denotes a truce or reconciliation. The example wadan ni naru begins here, with its verb continued on the next row.
Naru completes the example 'come to terms'. The Portuguese explains making peace or friendship, with a- beginning amizades below.

runs.text: mizades entre os que erão contrarios.

lines.note: Completes amizades and identifies the parties as people who were formerly opposed. The visible z corrects the OCR's migades; the line finishes the reconciliation example.
Wada no hara is the poetic expression for the sea, explicitly equated with umi. The poetry label and the independent Japanese synonym are retained in their respective printed styles.

The entry gives another poetic sea-name, glossed by umi and Idem. NINJAL's supplied headword index identifies Vadatçu, but an a between V and d is not securely visible in this copy; the provisional Vdatçu is retained with that damage caveat. Lexical aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html).

runs.text: O traduzir em lingua de Iapão: palaura

lines.note: Wahon is defined as translating into Japanese. The following words characterize it as a coined expression used in the Church rather than a general everyday headword.
Completes the editorial explanation that the word is constructed and used in the Church. The historical initial v of vſada is retained.
Waga is explained with first-person 'I', followed by a less proper second-person use. The Latin minùs is visible rather than the OCR's minis; pro- continues propriè below.

Completes the Latin qualification 'less properly' and the Portuguese pronoun Tu. The pronoun is printed upright here, though it belongs to Portuguese apparatus, not a Japanese span; Vagamono then illustrates something belonging to me, or in the extended use to you.
Completes the alternate possessive gloss 'or yours'. The short line belongs to wagamono and does not introduce another headword.

runs.text: Eu meſmo, ou minùs propriè, Tu

lines.note: Wagami means oneself, here 'I myself' and, less properly, 'you yourself'. The scan supports propriè, correcting OCR proprid, and retains the Latin qualification inside the italic explanation.
Completes Tu meſmo, 'you yourself', in the less proper second-person use of wagami. It remains its own physical row.
Wagaseko is identified as a poetic expression meaning 'my husband'. The gloss supplies that relationship directly, without replacing the historical form with a modern equivalent.

runs.text: Taboas que ſeruem de telhas pera cu-

lines.note: Wage denotes wooden boards serving as roofing tiles. The scan's telhas corrects OCR telbas, while cu- begins the historical verb cubrir on the next row.

runs.text: brir as caſas: no Cami ſe diz Cure.

lines.note: Completes covering houses and states that the term is Cure in the Cami region. Cami and Cure are Japanese words embedded in Portuguese prose; the local sloping type is retained and the whole words are flagged for optional font review.

runs.text: Vague, uru, eta. l, Mague, uru, eta.

lines.note: Wageru and mageru are alternative verbs for making bent or rounded objects. The repeated uru, eta endings are principal forms, and the Latin l introduces the alternative headword.
The round objects include small boxes, made by bending wood. Bocetas is retained in its historical container sense; the next row describes joining the ends.

runs.text: & ajuntando as pontas das taboas delgadas.

lines.note: Completes the fabrication process by joining the ends of thin boards. The descending j in ajuntando corrects the OCR's auntando; the phrase remains entirely Portuguese italic.
Wagemono and magemono name the objects made by that bending process. Qualquer introduces the following definition of any such box or case.

runs.text: boceta, ou caixa feita deſta maneira.

lines.note: Completes the definition as a small box or case made in this fashion. Deſta maneira points back to bending and joining thin boards above.
Wage tamari introduces a snake's coiled posture. The abbreviated principal ending is retained as printed u; enroſ- continues the Portuguese adjective enroscada below.
Completes enroscada and begins the snake example: it had been coiled, but suddenly changed posture. The scan supports tamatte, correcting OCR tamarte; niua- continues niwakani at the top of column 2.
Cani completes niwakani across the column break: the snake suddenly became straight. The Portuguese begins by recalling that the snake had been coiled; enroſca- continues below.

runs.text: da, mas derepente ſe endireitou, & eſtendeo.

lines.note: Completes enroscada, then contrasts that posture with suddenly straightening and stretching out. The historical contiguous derepente and eſtendeo are retained.

Wagoo denotes joining or union, with the Japanese explanatory expression Yauaracanivǒ preceding the Portuguese gloss. The scan distinguishes its caron from the earlier circumflex in Vacugô; the close printed joining in Yauaracanivǒ is retained without inserting a conjectural word boundary.
Adds mixture, then illustrates the body formed by the union of the four elements. The visible u restores miſtura from OCR miſtara; Cor- begins corpo below.

runs.text: po humano compoſto dos quatro elementos vni-

lines.note: Completes corpo humano and explains the body as composed of four united elements. The line-end vni- continues unidos on the next physical row.
Dos completes unidos. Anima and shikitai then illustrate the union of soul and body; Anima is incorporated into the upright example, while italic V- begins the Portuguese infinitive unir-se below.

runs.text: nirſe a alma, & o corpo como forma, & ma-

lines.note: Completes unirſe and gives the soul-body relation as form and matter. The final ma- is Portuguese materia, not a fragment of the Japanese example.

runs.text: teria. ¶ Permet. Fazerſe amigo cõ alguem.

lines.note: Completes materia, with t rather than the OCR's r. The figurative extension is becoming someone's friend; the abbreviation Permet. and cõ are preserved without expansion in the transcription.
Wago is a Japanese word, directly translated as palaura de Iapão. The absence of a vowel mark distinguishes this entry from the preceding union sense.

runs.text: Vos, abaixando hum pouco a peßoa cõ

lines.note: Wagoze is a second-person address described as lowering the addressee somewhat. The gloss explicitly comments on interpersonal register, rather than merely offering a neutral pronoun.
Completes 'the person with whom one speaks', identifying the recipient of the preceding lowering form of address. This short continuation ends the vagoje entry.
Wagon is presented as a musical instrument compared with a rabeca. The historical comparison is transcribed as printed and is not replaced with a modern organological definition.

runs.text: Modo de tremer com medo, ou

lines.note: Wajiwajito describes a manner of trembling from fear or cold. The gi spellings are normal material for contextual Japanese reading and are not modernized to ji.
Completes the cold/fear alternatives and supplies wajiwajito furuu, to tremble in that manner. The caron in furǔ and the italic Vt are visible.
Completes the explanatory phrase 'in this manner'. It points back to the preceding mimetic adverb and its trembling example.

runs.text: Camude de junco que ajuda a gouer-

lines.note: Waikaji names a rudder aid made of reed material. Enlargement supports the apparent printed Camude, which is retained despite its lexical peculiarity rather than silently substituting canudo; the following clause unambiguously states that it helps to steer the rudder.
Nar completes gouernar: the reed component helps govern or steer the rudder. The short continuation supplies the object leme and ends this nautical entry.

runs.text: Armas que ſe poem de baixo dos bra-

lines.note: Waidate denotes protective armor positioned below the arms. The Portuguese armas is contextualized as armor by its placement under the arms or armpits in the next row.
Ços completes braços and the alternate phrase specifies the armpits. The printed ſouacos, including its initial long s, is retained.
Wairo is equated with mainai and glossed as bribes or bribery. Va- starts the example wairo wo toru, divided across this physical line break.
Completes wairo wo toru, 'take bribes', exactly matching tomar peitas. The second example begins wairo ni, whose verb alternatives follow below.
Fukeru and mezzuru are alternatives for being drawn into or influenced by bribery. The Latin l separates the alternatives; the Portuguese gloss continues after 'or'.

Completes being led by bribes and begins an example of treating an unjust case as right because of bribery. The initial V of Vaironi has the conspicuously sloping form retained from the aligned OCR; the remaining example is upright.
Completes the example's unjust matter being made right, with ri ni suru as its predicate. The Portuguese translates the motive as bribes or self-interest; juſti- continues justificar below.
Completes justificar and identifies its object as an unjust lawsuit or claim. The scan supports demanda, correcting OCR demauda, while retaining the historical long-s forms.

runs.text: Vento Noroeſte, ou qualquer outro que

lines.note: Waita is defined as a northwest wind, then more broadly as another wind between principal bearings. The capitalized Noroeſte and printed long s are retained.
Completes the broader definition: a wind blowing between two principal compass directions. The historical dous and principaes are not modernized.
Wameki and its principal forms describe shouting or making a disturbance. The abbreviated u, eita endings are preserved as printed; traquina- begins the Portuguese noun completed below.
Completes traquinada and specifies speaking loudly. The scan supports falando, with f rather than OCR long s; wameki sakebu then gives a Japanese shouting example.

Bradar translates crying out. The next example adds soodoo suru, making a noisy disturbance, whose Portuguese explanation continues below; both vowel marks are preserved according to their printed direction.
Completes the shouting-and-disturbance example with making a commotion or bustle. The two Portuguese nouns reinforce the noisy-action sense.
Wan is explained as a bowl having a rounded rim, expressed by tamabuchi no aru wo yuu nari. The explanatory Japanese remains upright; Hũa starts the Portuguese description below.

runs.text: laya de eſcudelas de pao vruxadas que tem hũ

lines.note: The bowls are wooden and lacquered, with a feature specified next. The printed vruxadas incorporates the lacquer term into Portuguese morphology, so it is retained as part of the italic explanation.

runs.text: vinco, ou maneira de debrum pollas bordas de

lines.note: Describes a ridge or binding-like edging along the bowl's rim. The continuation de cima on the next row places that edging around the upper border.
Completes the description of the upper rim all around. Xǒjiuan introduces a particular form of bowl associated with the monks' vegetable diet, with Eſcude- starting the Portuguese plural below.

runs.text: lus de hũa certa feição differente das outras, em

lines.note: Completes the divided bowl-name and says these bowls have a particular shape different from others. Enlargement supports printed lus after Eſcude-, an apparent anomaly against expected las; the visible u is preserved rather than silently correcting the source.

runs.text: que comem os Bonzos que não comem peixe,

lines.note: The bowls are used by monks who do not eat fish. Bonzos is Portuguese vocabulary for the monks, not a Japanese citation or headword requiring a typeface-term flag.
Completes the dietary explanation as eating nothing beyond herbs or vegetables and the like. The text characterizes the users of these bowls, not their material.
Wana means a snare or trap, glossed with several trapping devices. Louza is retained in the printed list; Vt introduces a trapped-in-a-snare example.
Wana ni kakaru means getting caught in a snare or trap. The Portuguese cair no laço matches the Japanese intransitive construction.
Wana wo kakuru is setting a trap, contrasted with getting caught in one on the preceding row. The Portuguese ra- starts ratoeira below.
Completes ratoeira and gives another trap-setting phrase, wana wo sasu. Its Portuguese gloss turns specifically to setting traps for birds; paſ- continues the bird noun below.
Completes paſſaros and identifies snares or abuys as the trapping devices. The unusual printed abuys is retained, without modernizing its spelling or adding a more specific device identification.
Wananaki, wananaqu and its past form describe trembling from cold or fear. The abbreviated principal forms qu and aita belong to the headword's morphology and are preserved.
Completes the fear alternative and gives furui wananaku as a synonymous expression for trembling. Idem refers to the same cold-or-fear sense.
Wanawanato is an adverb describing a manner of trembling. Adu. explicitly identifies its grammatical use; the example follows on the next physical row.
Wanawanato furuu completes the example 'tremble in that manner'. The short upright example is the last body row; the lower Vana- is separate catchword furniture.
